Hi everyone! Our AI4Math team at BICMR@PKU, led by Prof. Bin Dong, is pleased to present Shouyi, a human-in-the-loop AI-agent workflow dedicated to the continuous refinement of Mathlib. Our workflow facilitates the systematic resolution of widely distributed technical debt and repository maintenance by surfacing actionable candidates, effectively scaling these traditionally tedious works beyond manual constraints. The agent operates strictly as a candidate generator subject to expert review, rather than an autonomous maintainer.

Core Maintenance Directions

These four directions serve as initial application examples of our scanning methodology; the workflow is not limited to these areas and can be extended to address a broader range of maintenance challenges within Mathlib.

  • Proof Golf: Discovering opportunities to reuse existing infrastructure to construct shorter proofs.

  • Assumption Weakening: Detecting and eliminating assumptions that are not logically required by the theorem.

  • erw Elimination: Repairing erw technical debt without introducing new defeq abuses.

  • Docstring Repair: Identifying and correcting outdated documentation that diverges from the underlying declarations.

Empirical Results

  • Proof Golf: Initial evaluations targeted the Analysis, NumberTheory, and MeasureTheory directories. Over 50 mathematically meaningful optimization PRs have been successfully merged into Mathlib. For the complete list, please see the dependencies in index PRs #37968, #38104, and #38144.

  • erw Elimination: Targeted over 600 erw instances repository-wide. Over 50 resolutions merged to date. See index PR #38415.

  • Assumption Weakening: Evaluated 1102 files within the Category Theory domain, identifying 77 candidate files (9 pure assumption deletions, 68 partial weakenings).

  • Docstring Repair: Evaluated 500 files within the Category Theory domain, with approximately 40% of the flagged occurrences demonstrating semantically meaningful corrections.

Detailed reports and illustrative examples are provided in the attachment below.

shouyi_report.pdf

We have open-sourced our prompts and parallel scanning scripts and welcome your rigorous review and feedback.
GitHub: https://github.com/frenzymath/shouyi

AI4M Team, BICMR@PKU

For assumption weakening, it's important to note that in general we only want to weaken typeclass assumptions where this is mathematically meaningful, or at least makes it genuinely more convenient to use the lemma. Sometimes weaker assumptions are unhelpful because in fact together with the other hypotheses they imply the stronger assumptions, or the only extra cases they cover are mathematically uninteresting, or a definition is right with the stronger assumptions but would need larger changes to be the proper generalization to weaker assumptions.

@Yi.Yuan Wow, the shouyi report looks very promising. I think the golfs in #37968 are really solid and it's good to see them being merged. I think examples like the "short helper lemma" in appendix 5.1 are also really good PRs. I am skeptical of the "68 partial assumption weakenings in CategoryTheory." That folder is very intentionally designed, and as Myers points out, sometimes it's important not to over-generalize.

Your goals are very admirable. As you write in the abstract, "We argue that the value of this workflow is to extend the reach of human maintainers and make the upkeep of large formal libraries more scalable and systematic." As long as it is still a human-in-loop calling the shots (and there is critical awareness of our AI use), I think these approaches can help perform a lot of menial chores, potentially freeing contributors to worry about higher-level architectural decisions. I greatly look forward to your plan "to organize more examples and report the relevant cases back to the Lean and Mathlib communities in a cleaner form."
@Yi.Yuan do you have representative examples of the assumption-refactorings? Have any of these already been PR'd / merged?

In our previous tests, we didn't focus on assumption weakening — it was just a byproduct of golfing. However, we later realized that assumption weakening has the potential to become a main feature, so we also included it in the report. Current examples include: #37555, #37737, #38353, #38298, and https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/38104/changes#diff-8f79fbf7346b7298cd848969f742557d492af7db05ceb20174f9e966665e8615 (sub-PR not yet opened).
The four examples here look good to me

I think later I can add a filtering condition to the gating: theorems with strictly fewer arguments, i.e., the modified theorem can imply the original theorem, but the original theorem cannot imply the modified one.

Actually, #38298 might be a case of "important redundant data". The [HasPushout f f] [HasPullback f.op f.op] can be golfed, but there are 4 other signatures like that in the file. The dependence on pushout+pullback explicitly may be to remind users that the conclusions of the theorem depend on both instances.
I believe there may also be cases where adding redundant typeclasses like this can improve synth performance, so you should also add -perf call to your filter/gating system
